title: 1 Samuel 22:6–19
context: Saul, sitting with spear in hand among his Benjamite officials, accuses them of conspiring with David and Jonathan. Doeg the Edomite reports what he saw at Nob. Saul summons Ahimelech and the priests; Ahimelech protests his innocence, but Saul condemns them all. When Saul's guards refuse to strike the priests of the LORD, Doeg kills eighty-five priests and then destroys the town of Nob. The narrator records this atrocity soberly, as the act of a king who has turned against God.

verses.text: Saul heard that David was discovered, with the men who were with him. Now Saul was sitting in Gibeah, under the tamarisk tree in Ramah, with his spear in his hand, and all his servants were standing around him.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul sits under the tamarisk with his spear in hand. Arminian readers see a king consumed by suspicion, his spear a sign of the violence that has marked his reign since the LORD's Spirit departed from him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the spear has appeared before, thrown at David (18:11). Saul's grip on it symbolizes his clutching at a kingdom God has already taken from him, a picture of rule without grace.

verses.text: Saul said to his servants who stood around him, “Hear now, you Benjamites! Will the son of Jesse give everyone of you fields and vineyards? Will he make you all captains of thousands and captains of hundreds?
verses.arminianNotes: Saul appeals to tribal loyalty: will the son of Jesse give Benjamites fields and commands? Arminian readers see a leader trying to hold power through patronage and fear rather than faithfulness to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Saul's appeal reveals what his kingship has become: a system of rewards and favors. His rule rests on human loyalty, while David's rests on God's choice.

verses.text: Is that why all of you have conspired against me, and there is no one who discloses to me when my son makes a treaty with the son of Jesse, and there is none of you who is sorry for me, or discloses to me that my son has stirred up my servant against me, to lie in wait, as it is today?”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul accuses his servants of conspiracy and complains that no one is sorry for him. Arminian readers see self-pity and paranoia that twist reality, as Saul treats his son's friendship as a plot against him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see how sin distorts perception. Saul casts himself as the victim while pursuing an innocent man, showing the blindness that comes when a person persistently resists God.

verses.text: Then Doeg the Edomite, who stood by the servants of Saul, answered and said, “I saw the son of Jesse coming to Nob, to Ahimelech the son of Ahitub.
verses.arminianNotes: Doeg the Edomite speaks up, reporting that he saw David at Nob with Ahimelech. Arminian readers note that Doeg chooses to inform, seeking favor with the king, and his choice leads to terrible bloodshed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the heading of Psalm 52, which names Doeg's report to Saul. Scripture holds Doeg fully responsible, and that psalm contrasts the boasting of evil men with God's enduring loving kindness.

verses.text: He inquired of the LORD for him, gave him food, and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine.”
verses.arminianNotes: Doeg says Ahimelech "inquired of the LORD for him," a detail chapter 21 does not record. Arminian readers note that Doeg's report shapes the facts to cast the priest as a conspirator, whatever actually happened.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same gap; the narrative may simply be selective, or Doeg may be embellishing. Either way, his testimony is weaponized to accuse an innocent man of treason.

verses.text: Then the king sent to call Ahimelech the priest, the son of Ahitub, and all his father’s house, the priests who were in Nob; and they all came to the king.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul summons Ahimelech and "all his father's house, the priests who were in Nob." Arminian readers see the king's anger extending to an entire family, a sign of how unchecked power devours the innocent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the priests are descendants of Eli (14:3). God had warned Eli's house of judgment (2:31–33), and the narrator places this tragedy within that long story without excusing Saul.

verses.text: Saul said, “Hear now, you son of Ahitub.” He answered, “Here I am, my lord.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul calls him "son of Ahitub" rather than by name, and Ahimelech answers, "Here I am, my lord." Arminian readers note the priest's respectful submission, showing his loyalty to the king even under accusation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the cold address and the priest's humble reply. The exchange highlights Ahimelech's innocence and the injustice of what Saul is about to do to a faithful servant.

verses.text: Saul said to him, “Why have you conspired against me, you and the son of Jesse, in that you have given him bread, and a sword, and have inquired of God for him, that he should rise against me, to lie in wait, as it is today?”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul accuses Ahimelech of conspiring with David by giving him bread, a sword, and inquiring of God. Arminian readers note that Saul interprets ordinary acts of help as treason, reading his own fears into others.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Saul's charge repeats Doeg's version of events. False accusation, fed by an informer, becomes the basis for judgment, a pattern Scripture repeatedly condemns.

verses.text: Then Ahimelech answered the king, and said, “Who among all your servants is so faithful as David, who is the king’s son-in-law, captain of your body guard, and honored in your house?
verses.arminianNotes: Ahimelech defends David as the king's faithful son-in-law and captain of his bodyguard. Arminian readers admire his courage in speaking truth to an angry king, risking his life to defend an innocent man.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Ahimelech's defense of David is accurate and honorable. He bears witness to David's faithfulness at great personal cost, a righteous voice in an unrighteous court.

verses.text: Have I today begun to inquire of God for him? Be it far from me! Don’t let the king impute anything to his servant, nor to all the house of my father; for your servant knew nothing of all this, less or more.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ahimelech says he "knew nothing of all this." Arminian readers note that the priest was deceived by David's false story (21:2), so his ignorance was genuine, which deepens the guilt of those who harm him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Ahimelech's claim is true, as chapter 21 makes clear. His innocence highlights both Saul's injustice and the painful cost of David's earlier deception.

verses.text: The king said, “You shall surely die, Ahimelech, you and all your father’s house.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul pronounces death on Ahimelech and all his father's house. Arminian readers see a king who has abandoned justice entirely, condemning the innocent without evidence out of rage and fear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Saul, who failed to carry out God's judgment on Amalek (15:9), now commands slaughter of God's priests. His disobedience has turned his zeal against the very people he should protect.

verses.text: The king said to the guard who stood about him, “Turn and kill the priests of the LORD, because their hand also is with David, and because they knew that he fled and didn’t disclose it to me.” But the servants of the king wouldn’t put out their hand to fall on the priests of the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The guards refuse to "put out their hand to fall on the priests of the LORD." Arminian readers see conscience at work: the servants make a courageous moral choice to disobey an unjust order.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also commend the guards' refusal. They see God restraining evil through ordinary people who fear him, and a reminder that obedience to God outranks obedience to a ruler.

verses.text: The king said to Doeg, “Turn and attack the priests!” Doeg the Edomite turned, and he attacked the priests, and he killed on that day eighty-five people who wore a linen ephod.
verses.arminianNotes: Doeg the Edomite kills eighty-five priests who wore the linen ephod. Arminian readers see the horror of what one person's willingness to do evil can accomplish when others refuse, and hold Doeg fully guilty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrator records the number and their priestly garments soberly. Doeg acts freely and wickedly; Scripture lays the guilt on him and on Saul, while the event also relates to the word against Eli's house.

verses.text: He struck Nob, the city of the priests, with the edge of the sword—both men and women, children and nursing babies, and cattle, donkeys, and sheep, with the edge of the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: Nob is struck with the sword, including women, children, infants, and animals. Arminian readers note the bitter irony that Saul carries out against God's priests the destruction he failed to carry out against Amalek (15:3, 9).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same tragic reversal. Saul's refusal to obey God has become a willingness to destroy the innocent. Both traditions see here the darkness of a heart that has turned away from God.
